paras: The shooting of Dick Milner took place in Hickman, Kentucky, probably on Monday, January 30, 1882, when City Marshal Barnes shot Milner, a Black man, in the leg as he ran from arrest. The wound was reported as not dangerous, and the only known account is a brief item in the local Hickman Courier.

According to the Courier, Barnes was trying to handcuff Milner when Milner "gave show of resistance, and run." The marshal fired two shots after him, one of which struck him "in the fleshy part of the leg." The item does not say why Barnes was arresting Milner, where in town the shooting happened, or whether anyone else was present.

The Courier described the wound as "not dangerous" and printed nothing further about the case in this item; no report of a charge against Milner or of any inquiry into the shooting appears in the coverage.

The Hickman Courier ran the story on February 3, 1882, as a four-sentence paragraph in its local column, without a headline, between notes on a pump factory and corn awaiting shipment. The paper identified Milner as "a colored man" and gave the marshal's side of events, his resistance and flight, as the account of the shooting without comment. No other newspaper is known to have carried the story.
